# Block 4: Iterations with purrr {.unnumbered} *Roughly 55 minutes. First the `map` toolkit, then the same tools applied to the running example so that the three function calls from Block 3 become one pipeline.* The refactored script still has three explicit calls, one per species. A fourth species means a fourth call. Iteration removes the per-group calls entirely: the function is applied to each group automatically. ## Part A: the `map` toolkit `purrr::map(.x, .f)` applies the function `.f` to each element of `.x` and returns a list. It is the tidyverse counterpart of base R's `lapply()`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} vec_list <- list(a = 1:10, b = 11:20, c = 21:30) purrr::map(vec_list, mean) # a list of three means ``` ::: `map()` always returns a list, which is maximally general but often more than you want. The typed variants return an atomic vector and *fail* if the result is not of that type, which is a feature: it catches mistakes early. | Function | Returns | |---|---| | `map()` | a list | | `map_lgl()` | a logical vector | | `map_int()` | an integer vector | | `map_dbl()` | a double vector | | `map_chr()` | a character vector | ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} purrr::map_dbl(vec_list, mean) # a named numeric vector, not a list ``` ::: :::{.callout-note} This type-safety is the reason to prefer `map_*()` over base `sapply()`. `sapply()` guesses the output type and can return a vector, a matrix or a list depending on the input, so a function that worked on Tuesday can silently return a different shape on Wednesday. `map_dbl()` either returns a double vector or errors. Predictability beats convenience. ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The base R alternative: a `for` loop Before `map()`, the same job needs a loop with manual bookkeeping: pre-allocate an output container, then assign into it by index. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} vec_list <- list(a = 1:10, b = 11:20, c = 21:30) means <- vector("double", length(vec_list)) # pre-allocate data type and length names(means) <- names(vec_list) # carry names across by hand for (i in seq_along(vec_list)) { means[[i]] <- mean(vec_list[[i]]) } means ``` ::: `purrr::map_dbl(df_list, mean)` collapses all of this into one call. The loop is not wrong, and understanding it is worth doing, but three jobs are now yours rather than the function's: choosing the container type, sizing it, and preserving names. Growing the vector instead of pre-allocating (`means <- c(means, ...)` inside the loop) copies the whole object on every iteration, which turns linear work into quadratic and is the classic loop performance trap. `map_dbl()` handles the container, the sizing and the names, and fixes the return type. The honest contrast is delegated bookkeeping, not raw speed: a correctly pre-allocated loop and `map_dbl()` run in comparable time. ::: ### Anonymous functions: `\(x)`, and the `~` you will still see When the callback is not already a named function, write it inline. The modern form is the R 4.1 shorthand `\(x)`: :::{.panel-tabset} ## Updated ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} purrr::map_dbl(vec_list, \(x) sum(x) / length(x)) ``` ::: ## Original ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} purrr::map_dbl(vec_list, function(x) sum(x) / length(x)) ``` ::: ::: You will frequently meet the older purrr formula-lambda, `~ sum(.x) / length(.x)`, where `.x` (or `.`) stands for the current element. It still works, but `\(x)` is clearer because the argument has a real name, and it is ordinary R rather than purrr-specific syntax. We use `\(x)` throughout. Extra arguments can be passed either inside the lambda or as trailing arguments to `map()`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} purrr::map_dbl(vec_list, \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) # inside the lambda purrr::map_dbl(vec_list, mean, na.rm = TRUE) # forwarded by map() ``` ::: ### Returning a data frame: `map() |> list_rbind()` To stack per-element tibbles into one tibble, run `map()` and then `list_rbind()`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Example: files <- list.files(here::here("data", "many_files"), pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE) all_data <- files |> purrr::map(\(f) readr::read_csv(f, show_col_types = FALSE)) |> purrr::list_rbind() ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # --- Setup: write the penguins data out as several CSV files --- # In a real project these files would already exist; here we create them # so the reading example has something to read. We split by island, so # each file holds the penguins recorded at one location. dir.create(here("data", "many_files"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE) penguins_clean |> group_by(island) |> group_walk(\(rows, key) { write_csv(rows, here("data", "many_files", paste0(key$island, ".csv"))) }) # --- Reading the files back in --- files <- list.files(here("data", "many_files"), pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE) # example to show list format before rbind files |> map(\(f) read_csv(f, show_col_types = FALSE)) # combined dataframe all_data <- files |> map(\(f) read_csv(f, show_col_types = FALSE)) |> list_rbind() all_data ``` ::: :::{.callout-warning} You will see `map_dfr()` and `map_dfc()` in older code and tutorials. These are **superseded**: the current idiom is `map() |> list_rbind()` for row-binding and `map() |> list_cbind()` for column-binding. They are clearer about the two separate steps (apply, then combine) and are the forms the tidyverse now recommends. ::: ### The base R family, in one paragraph You will encounter `lapply()`, `sapply()`, `vapply()` and `apply()` in existing code, and parallel iteration via `foreach` or `furrr`. The translation is direct: `lapply(x, f)` is `map(x, f)`; `sapply(x, f)` is one of the typed `map_*()` variants depending on the return type. Parallel back-ends such as `furrr::future_map()` mirror `map()`'s interface for when a computation is genuinely slow and embarrassingly parallel. We mention these so you recognise them; for new code, `purrr` is the consistent default and parallelism is a later optimisation, applied only after profiling shows it is needed. ### `map2` and `pmap` and `imap`: iterating over more than one input `map2(.x, .y, .f)` walks two collections in parallel, passing one element from each to the function. `pmap(.l, .f)` generalises to any number of inputs, taking a list (or a data frame, treating each column as an input). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sizes <- c(2, 3, 4) widths <- c(5, 6, 7) purrr::map2_dbl(sizes, widths, \(s, w) s * w) # 10 18 28 ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sizes <- c(2, 3, 4) widths <- c(5, 6, 7) heights <- c(1, 2, 3) # pmap takes a list of vectors; each call receives one element from each. pmap_dbl(list(sizes, widths, heights), \(s, w, h) s * w * h) # 10 36 84 ``` ::: :::{.callout-note collapse = "true"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # pmap walks any number of inputs in parallel. A data frame is just a named # list of columns, so passing one lets each column become an argument. # The function's parameter names should match the column names. penguins_clean |> select(species, body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm) |> drop_na() |> slice_head(n = 3) |> pmap_chr(\(species, body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm) { glue::glue("{species}: Body weight {body_mass_g}g, Flipper length {flipper_length_mm}mm ") }) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae): Body weight 3750g, Flipper length 181mm " [2] "Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae): Body weight 3800g, Flipper length 186mm " [3] "Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae): Body weight 3250g, Flipper length 195mm " ``` ::: ::: ::: ### `walk`: iteration for side effects When you iterate to *do* something (write files, print plots) rather than to *return* a value, use `walk()`/`walk2()`. They run the function for its side effect and return their input invisibly, so the console is not flooded with output. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Write each split of the data to its own file, silently peng_split <- penguins_clean |> dplyr::group_by(species) |> dplyr::group_split() names(peng_split) <- c("Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo") purrr::walk2( peng_split, names(peng_split), \(data, nm) readr::write_csv(data, here::here("data", paste0(nm, ".csv"))) ) ``` ::: :::{.callout-note} Note the slightly different approach to walk, here we split the data into a list and used `walk` in a previous example we used `group_walk`a variant designed explicitly to work on data after `group_by` ::: ## Part B: iteration on the running example Recall the list-column from Block 2: `group_by(species) |> nest()` puts each species' tibble into one cell of a `data` column. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} species_data <- penguins_clean |> dplyr::group_by(species) |> tidyr::nest() species_data # # A tibble: 3 x 2 # species data # # 1 Adelie # 2 Gentoo # 3 Chinstrap ``` ::: :::{.callout-note} We use the classic `group_by() |> nest()` rather than the newer `nest(.by = species)`. Both give the same result; the explicit grouping step is clearer and backward-compatible. ::: ### Applying a function to each cell Used inside `mutate()`, `map()` applies a function to each cell of a list-column and stores the result as a new list-column: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} species_models <- species_data |> dplyr::mutate( model = purrr::map(data, \(d) lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = d)), coefs = purrr::map(model, \(m) broom::tidy(m, conf.int = TRUE)), n_obs = purrr::map_int(data, nrow) ) species_models # # A tibble: 3 x 5 # species data model coefs n_obs # # 1 Adelie 146 # 2 Gentoo 119 # 3 Chinstrap 68 ``` ::: Three things to notice. The `model` cell holds a fitted `lm` per species; the `coefs` cell holds a tidied tibble per species; and `n_obs` is an ordinary integer column, not a list-column, because `map_int()` returns an atomic vector. The typed variants slot straight into a tibble. ### Unnesting back to a flat table For a manuscript coefficient table, expand the `coefs` list-column back into rows. `unnest()` is the dual of `nest()`: each cell's tibble becomes rows, with the surrounding columns repeated. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} coefficient_table <- species_models |> dplyr::ungroup() |> dplyr::select(species, coefs) |> tidyr::unnest(coefs) ``` ::: ### A real refactor: decompose the function There is a tension. `fit_species_model()` filters *and* fits, but `nest()` has already done the filtering. Calling it inside the iteration would filter twice. That tension is information: the function is doing two jobs. Split them. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # R/functions/modelling_functions.R -- revised #' Fit body mass ~ flipper length on pre-filtered data #' @param data A data frame, assumed to be one species' worth. #' @return A fitted lm object. fit_model <- function(data) { lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = data) } #' Tidy a fitted lm with confidence intervals #' @param model A fitted lm object. #' @param conf_level Confidence level. Default 0.95. #' @return A tibble of tidied coefficients. tidy_model <- function(model, conf_level = 0.95) { broom::tidy(model, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = conf_level) } #' Fit for one species (wrapper preserving the old interface) #' @param data A data frame with a `species` column. #' @param sp Character of length 1. Species to filter to. #' @param conf_level Confidence level. Default 0.95. fit_species_model <- function(data, sp, conf_level = 0.95) { if (!sp %in% unique(data$species)) { stop("Species '", sp, "' is not in the data. ", "Available species: ", paste(sort(unique(data$species)), collapse = ", ")) } data |> dplyr::filter(species == sp) |> fit_model() |> tidy_model(conf_level = conf_level) |> dplyr::mutate(species = sp, .before = 1) } ``` ::: `fit_model()` and `tidy_model()` now exist independently and compose. The old public interface survives as a wrapper, so existing callers and the tests from Block 3 still pass with no edits. That is what a good refactor looks like: behaviour preserved, internals improved, tests green. ### The iteration, rewritten With single-responsibility functions, the iteration uses them directly and reads cleanly: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} species_models <- penguins_clean |> dplyr::group_by(species) |> tidyr::nest() |> dplyr::mutate( model = purrr::map(data, fit_model), coefs = purrr::map(model, tidy_model) ) coefficient_table <- species_models |> dplyr::ungroup() |> dplyr::select(species, coefs) |> tidyr::unnest(coefs) ``` ::: This is the destination. The modelling logic that was three copy-pasted blocks in Block 1, then three function calls in Block 3, is now one pipeline that applies the same function to every group. ### Activity: iterate over a different grouping :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} iterate over a different grouping :::: ::::{.task-container} The penguins data has an `island` column ("Biscoe", "Dream", "Torgersen"). Fit a separate `body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm` model for each island and produce a tidied coefficient table, using the nest pattern. :::: :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} island_coefs <- penguins_clean |> dplyr::group_by(island) |> tidyr::nest() |> dplyr::mutate( model = purrr::map(data, fit_model), coefs = purrr::map(model, tidy_model) ) |> dplyr::ungroup() |> dplyr::select(island, coefs) |> tidyr::unnest(coefs) ``` ::: `fit_model()` and `tidy_model()` are reused unchanged. They never knew they would iterate over species; they work for islands too, because each has a single responsibility and no hidden assumption about the grouping.
### Extension exercise: plots in a list-column :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Extension exercise: plots in a list-column :::: ::::{.task-container} A list-column can hold plots as readily as models. Using the nested data, add a `plot` column made with `map()` that holds one scatter plot per species, then draw them together with `patchwork::wrap_plots()`. Hint: build each plot inside `\(d) ggplot(d, ...)`. :::: :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} species_plots <- penguins_clean |> dplyr::group_by(species) |> tidyr::nest() |> dplyr::mutate( plot = purrr::map(data, \(d) ggplot2::ggplot(d, ggplot2::aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g)) + ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.6) + ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm") + ggplot2::theme_minimal()) ) patchwork::wrap_plots(species_plots$plot) ``` ::: The same `nest |> mutate(map(...))` pattern that fits models also builds figures. Once you see a cell as "any R object", models, plots and tables are all just list-columns.
:::{.callout-note} **Where this leaves us.** Copy-paste is gone. One pipeline fits a model per group, whatever the group is. But `fit_model()` still hardcodes the response and predictor: it only ever fits body mass on flipper length. Block 5 removes that last limitation. :::
